title: Weight-based oral doses: mg/kg and micrograms/kg then volume
blurb: Turn a mg/kg or micrograms/kg prescription into a dose, then into a volume or a number of tablets.
question: A child weighing 16 kg is prescribed paracetamol 15 mg/kg. The oral suspension is labelled 120 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given?

teach.body: Formal rule: dose = dose per kg × weight in kg; then volume = (dose ÷ stock strength) × stock volume (or tablets = dose ÷ tablet strength). Plain English: first find how much drug this person needs for their size, then measure that amount. Weight-based items appear on adult, children's, LD and MH practice papers.
teach.cite: FACTS.md section 4 (weight-based dose); Pearson VUE NMC practice papers

teach.h: Worked example: Amara in the children's emergency department
teach.body: Amara, 4, weighs 16 kg and is prescribed paracetamol 15 mg/kg. The suspension is 120 mg/5 mL. Step 1: dose = 15 × 16 = 240 mg. Step 2: volume = 240 ÷ 120 × 5 = 10 mL. Sense-check: 240 mg is twice 120 mg, so twice 5 mL. Type 10 mL.

teach.text: micrograms/kg against a mg label: 700 micrograms/kg × 12 kg = 8400 micrograms, which is 8.4 mg, not 8400 mg. Convert before dividing by the label strength, or the volume is a thousand times too big.

teach.caption: Divided daily doses have their own lesson.

teach.body: Do not round the calculated dose before working out the volume. Carry the full figure through and round the final volume to the decimal places asked. Children's papers often ask for two decimal places.

items: Dose = dose per kg × weight in kg.
Convert grams of body weight to kg first.
Match micrograms and mg before dividing by the label.
Then volume = dose ÷ strength × stock volume.

summary: You can now calculate a weight-based oral dose from mg/kg or micrograms/kg and turn it into a volume or a number of tablets. You can also avoid the classic errors of skipping the weight step and missing a micrograms conversion.

A.q: A child weighing 18 kg is prescribed paracetamol 15 mg/kg. The oral suspension is labelled 120 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.

whyNot.0: Forgot to multiply by the 5 mL stock volume.
whyNot.2: Forgot to multiply by the weight: used 15 mg as the dose.
whyNot.3: Rounded to one decimal place; the stem asks for two.

A.q: A person weighing 70 kg is prescribed a medicine at 0.5 mg/kg. What dose should be given in mg?

whyNot.0: Divided weight by dose per kg instead of multiplying.
whyNot.1: Forgot to multiply by the weight.
whyNot.2: Read 0.5 mg as 5 mg, a tenfold slip.

A.q: A client weighing 60 kg is prescribed sodium valproate 10 mg/kg. The oral solution is labelled 200 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit.

whyNot.1: Forgot to multiply by the 5 mL stock volume.
whyNot.2: Forgot to multiply by the weight.
whyNot.3: Weight taken as 600 kg, a tenfold slip.

B.q: A child weighing 12 kg is prescribed a medicine at 700 micrograms/kg. The oral solution is labelled 2 mg/mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.

whyNot.0: No conversion: 8400 micrograms divided by 2 mg.
whyNot.1: Forgot to multiply by the weight.
whyNot.3: 8400 micrograms was taken as 84 mg, a tenfold slip.

B.q: A person weighing 80 kg is prescribed a medicine at 0.25 mg/kg. The tablets available contain 10 mg each. How many tablets should be given?

whyNot.1: Forgot to multiply by the weight.
whyNot.2: Divided weight by dose per kg, giving 320 mg.
whyNot.3: Used the weight in kg as the dose in mg.

B.q: A baby weighing 4200 g is prescribed a medicine at 10 mg/kg. The oral solution is labelled 50 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.

whyNot.0: Left the weight in grams: 1000 times too much.
whyNot.1: Forgot to multiply by the 5 mL stock volume.
whyNot.2: Forgot to multiply by the weight.

C.q: A person weighing 68 kg is prescribed a medicine at 7.5 mg/kg. The oral suspension is labelled 250 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.

whyNot.0: Rounded the dose to 500 mg before calculating: rounding too early.
whyNot.2: Forgot to multiply by the 5 mL stock volume.
whyNot.3: Forgot to multiply by the weight.

C.q: A child weighing 22 kg is prescribed a medicine at 50 micrograms/kg. The oral solution is labelled 1 mg/mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.

whyNot.0: No conversion: 1100 micrograms treated as mg.
whyNot.1: Forgot to multiply by the weight.
whyNot.3: 1100 micrograms taken as 11 mg, a tenfold slip.

C.q: A client weighing 54 kg is prescribed a medicine at 15 mg/kg twice a day. The oral solution is labelled 200 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given for each dose? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.

whyNot.1: This is the daily volume, not each dose.
whyNot.2: Forgot to multiply by the 5 mL stock volume.
whyNot.3: Rounded to one decimal place; the stem asks for two.

reteach.title: Size first, then measure
reteach.question: A child weighs 20 kg and is prescribed 10 mg/kg. What dose is that?

blocks.body: mg/kg means "this many mg for every kg". A 20 kg child at 10 mg/kg needs 10 × 20 = 200 mg. Only then go to the bottle label.

blocks.text: Using 10 mg (the per-kg figure) as the dose gives 0.2 mL: twenty times too little.

explain.body: Dose = dose per kg × weight in kg. Multiply, never divide.

test.q: A child weighing 25 kg is prescribed a medicine at 4 mg/kg. What dose should be given in mg?

whyNot.0: Divided weight by dose per kg.
whyNot.1: Forgot to multiply by the weight.
whyNot.2: Weight taken as 250 kg, a tenfold slip.

test.q: A baby weighing 3600 g is prescribed a medicine at 2 mg/kg. What dose should be given in mg?

whyNot.0: Left the weight in grams: 1000 times too much.
whyNot.2: Divided weight by dose per kg.
whyNot.3: Forgot to multiply by the weight.

explain.body: Use the dose from step 1 as WANT: volume = dose ÷ label mg × label volume.

test.q: A child weighing 14 kg is prescribed a medicine at 5 mg/kg. The oral suspension is labelled 100 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.

whyNot.0: Forgot to multiply by the 5 mL stock volume.
whyNot.1: Forgot to multiply by the weight.
whyNot.3: Used 50 mg/5 mL, not the 100 mg/5 mL on the label.

test.q: A person weighing 60 kg is prescribed a medicine at 5 micrograms/kg. What is the dose in mg? Write your answer to one decimal place.

whyNot.1: Gave the micrograms figure as mg.
